prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Other weddings are so shrewd on the sofa, short and baffled, bassett-legged. All things knuckled, I have no winter left, in my sore rememory, to melt down for drinking water. Shrunk down. Your wedding slides the way wiry dark hairs do, down a swimming pool drain. So I am drained. Sincerely. I wish you every chapped bird on this pilgrimage to hold your hem up from the dust. Dust is plural: infinite dust. I will sink in the sun, I will crawl towards the heavy drawing and design the curtains in the room of never marrying you. Because it is a sinking, because today’s perfect weather is a later life’s smut. This soiled future unplans love. I keep unplanning the same Sunday. Leg and flower, breeze and terrier, I have no garden and couldn’t be happier. Please, don’t lose me here. I am sorry my clutch is all tendon and no discipline: the heart is a severed kind of muscle and alone. I can hear yours in your room. I hear mine in another room. In another’s.

outputs.L2:
Different weddings appear sly and low to the ground, stunted and perplexed, their legs stubby like a basset hound's. Everything has become gnarled and swollen-jointed; nothing remains within my aching memory to thaw into something drinkable. Everything has withered. Your marriage descends the way coarse dark strands disappear down a pool's drain—and so I too am emptied out. Truly. May every weather-worn bird accompany this journey and lift your garment's edge above the grime. And grime multiplies endlessly—dust upon dust without limit.

I will settle downward beneath the sun's weight, dragging myself toward some elaborate blueprint, arranging drapes for a chamber where our union never occurs. This is a descent, after all—because the flawless weather of today becomes tomorrow's stain, a corrupted future that dismantles what love might have been. Each Sunday I take apart again, the same one, over and over.

Limb and blossom, gust of wind and small dog—I possess no garden, yet contentment finds me anyway. Please don't abandon me in this moment. Forgive me—my grasp is nothing but raw sinew, lacking any restraint; the heart functions as a cut-off muscle, isolated. Yours beats audibly from your room. Mine sounds from elsewhere. From somewhere else entirely.
outputs.L3:
# On Weddings That Are Not My Own

There is a particular kind of ache that comes from standing at the edge of someone else's happiness, watching it unfold like a bruise blooming beneath skin. Other people's weddings arrive dressed in white lies of comfort—the too-tight collar of a borrowed suit, the way new shoes blister heels raw by the second dance, the champagne that turns sour in a stomach clenched too tight to celebrate freely. I have learned to smile through these events the way one learns to walk on a sprained ankle: carefully, with a wince disguised as joy.

My body knows before my mind admits it—this discomfort is not about the wedding at all.

---

I feel myself emptying, the way water finds every possible exit from a vessel that was never meant to hold it forever. There is a slow drain to grief that mimics the mundane: hair sliding reluctant and dark down porcelain, swirling in that final spiral before disappearing entirely. I am becoming less each day, sediment left behind after everything fluid has gone. This is what exhaustion looks like when it has nowhere left to go—not dramatic, not sudden, just the quiet math of subtraction happening in the pipes beneath ordinary life.

---

And still, I offer you blessings. I mean them, even as they cost me something to give.

May your life together be soft in all the right places. May you never know the particular grief of almost. But here, in this space between my teeth and the world, I confess: I never thought it would be someone else standing where I imagined myself. The vows I once rehearsed in silence were never meant for this altar, this light, this version of forever.

There is no contradiction in wishing you well and wishing, too, that things had been different. Both truths can live in the same chest, taking turns breathing.

---

Perhaps this is simply what happens to perfect moments—they cannot stay pristine. Time moves its thumb across even the clearest surface, leaving smudges where clarity used to live. We make plans in the language of certainty: *someday*, *when we're ready*, *after this next thing passes*—and then watch them curdle into disappointment, patient and recurring as tide.

I have lived this cycle before. The soiling is not an accident but an inevitability, the way fruit left in a bowl too long becomes something other than what it promised to be at the store. Perfect moments are perishable. We forget this until we're holding the proof in our hands, sticky and unsalvageable.

---

The heart, I've come to believe, works alone. It is a muscle without discipline, contracting and releasing on its own schedule, indifferent to the architecture we build around it. Yours beats in one room; mine in another. We have lived separate emotional lives even when we shared the same address, the same bed, the same Tuesday mornings—two rhythms occupying adjacent spaces, occasionally synchronizing by accident rather than design.

This is perhaps the quietest tragedy: that closeness was never the same as unity. That two hearts can occupy the same house and still keep entirely different hours, mourning what never had the chance to align.
outputs.L4:
# Untitled

The bells ring, and I am drowning in the sound of them.

Somewhere behind my ribs, something empties out—slowly, like water finding the smallest crack in a vessel, like sand through fingers that forgot how to close. I watch her walk toward a future that was never going to be mine, wrapped in white, wrapped in promises I used to whisper into the dark, thinking they were meant for me.

They weren't.

The room tilts. Or maybe I am the one tilting, sinking into the polished floor while everyone else remains upright, remains *present*, remains capable of clapping at the right moments. I clap too. My hands know the motion even as the rest of me dissolves into something that no longer resembles a person—more like dust caught in a shaft of light, visible only when it catches, invisible the moment it settles.

I keep waiting to wake up from this.

There is a version of me that exists somewhere else, in some other unfolding of time, standing where the groom stands now. That version knows a happiness I will never touch. I can almost see him—transparent, laughing, reaching for a hand that was never going to be mine to hold in this life. He fades when I try to look directly at him, the way stars do, the way everything I want seems to when I turn my full attention toward it.

My heart is behaving strangely—not breaking so much as *separating*, as though some invisible surgeon has severed it clean from the rest of my body and left it beating somewhere in a corner of the room, small and useless, still keeping time to a song no one else can hear. I feel its rhythm from a distance, feel my own pulse as a foreign thing, borrowed, ticking down toward nothing in particular.

The vows are being spoken. I catch fragments—*forsaking all others, until death, I do*—and each phrase lands like sediment, another layer of sand burying whatever future I thought I might have had. I try to imagine tomorrow and find only static, only white noise where plans used to live. What is there to look forward to when the thing I was looking forward to has just been given to someone else, sealed with a kiss, sealed with law and ceremony and the quiet finality of *chosen*?

I am not chosen.

I am the dust in the corner of this bright room, settling now that the light has moved on. I am the sand that slipped through some cosmic hourglass and landed in the wrong hour altogether. I am watching myself from outside my own body, a stranger observing a stranger, wondering why this particular grief feels so much like disappearing.

The reception begins. There is cake, there is laughter, there is a band playing something slow and sweet. I stand at the edges of it all, hollowed, drained, my heart still ticking somewhere apart from me, still isolated, still alone in its small corner—keeping time for a life that split off from mine long before I understood I'd lost anything at all.
outputs.L5:
# The Space Between Other and All

There is a peculiar geometry to human experience, one where we constantly measure ourselves against two impossible poles: the vastness of *All* and the isolation of being *Other*.

We spend our lives yearning to belong to the All—to feel part of something larger, to dissolve our individual edges into a collective identity. We want to be included in humanity's grand narrative, to matter within the totality of existence. Yet the moment we achieve any distinction, any individuality worth having, we simultaneously become the Other—separate, distinct, sometimes isolated by the very qualities that make us who we are.

This tension has shrunk many people into smaller versions of themselves. Fear of being labeled "other" causes some to compress their authentic selves into more palatable, acceptable shapes. They shrink their opinions, their appearances, their ambitions—anything that might mark them as different from the presumed All, the majority, the accepted norm.

But there's a quiet rebellion available to us: what if being Other isn't diminishment at all? What if the very act of being distinct, of standing apart from the All, is not a shrinking but an expansion? The people who have changed history were rarely those who blended seamlessly into everything else. They were the others—the ones who refused to shrink themselves to fit expectations.

Perhaps the real tragedy isn't being other to the all, but allowing that otherness to shrink us rather than define us with pride. The All doesn't need uniform pieces; it needs the vivid, unshrunk truth of every different thread that makes up its fabric. Our otherness, fully inhabited rather than shrunk into hiding, might be exactly what completes the whole.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, emotionally raw prose poem about attending an ex's wedding, using strange body-based imagery and fragmented syntax.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Guest Book

I sign my name with the hand that used to fit inside yours like a key finally finding its lock. Now it's just a hand. Now it's just skin remembering skin, which is the cruelest kind of memory—the kind with nerve endings.

You look beautiful. I mean it the way you mean it when you say *break a leg*—violence dressed as blessing.

Someone hands me champagne and I drink it like it's the year we spent learning each other's mouths, all that fizz and burn, gone flat before the toast even starts. My throat is a hallway you used to walk down. Now strangers' voices echo there instead.

I watch you say *I do* and feel my ribs rearrange themselves into a cage for something that already flew away. This is not metaphor. This is anatomy. Grief has its own skeleton and it's wearing my clothes tonight.

The DJ plays *our song* except it isn't anymore—songs are promiscuous like that, they'll marry anyone who asks. I dance with your cousin whose hands are wrong in ways I can't name but feel in my molars.

Your new husband's laugh sounds like a door I'll never be let back through. I keep checking my pulse against the wall, wondering which one of us stopped first.

In the bathroom mirror I don't recognize the face wearing my expression. It's borrowed. It's been borrowed since the day you left, and I keep expecting someone to ask for it back.

Outside, the moon is doing that thing where it looks like a wound healing wrong—too round, too white, too much like the ring on your finger that isn't the one I almost bought.

I eat the cake. It tastes like nothing. It tastes like the years I spent building a house out of your name and now I'm just standing in the wreckage, fork in hand, smiling for photographs.

Congratulations. I mean it the way skin means it right before it splits.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness poem about heartbreak and jealousy at someone else's wedding, blending domestic imagery (curtains, gardens, dust) with bodily metaphors.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Curtains Know

the lace was her idea, wasn't it, that pattern
of holes pretending to be flowers, and I am
sitting in the third pew with my ribs
doing origami, folding smaller, smaller,
a paper crane no one asked for—

the roses on the altar, someone grew those,
someone knelt in dirt with bleeding knees
and thought *this is for someone else's joy*
the way I water windowsill basil
that dies anyway, that always dies,

my hands remember his hands
like a house remembers a fire
even after renovation—
the smoke smell in the walls,
the way you sand and sand and sand
but the grain still darkens where it burned

her dress moves like curtains do
when someone leaves a window open,
that domestic breath, that in-and-out,
and I think of my own bedroom,
dust motes performing their slow ballet
in afternoon light, how dust is just
skin, is just what we shed and forget,

is this jealousy or is it grief
wearing a borrowed veil—
my stomach a garden gone to seed,
weeds where I planted *okay* and *moving on*,
my throat a drawer stuck shut
with everything I didn't say

she catches the bouquet and laughs
and I think of my own hands, empty,
always empty, reaching for stems
that were never thrown my direction,

the organ swells like something
underwater, like drowning
set to music, and I clap
because that's what mouths do
even when the heart
is just another room
in a house that's slowly, quietly,
being sold

## दिल टूटने और जलन की स्ट्रीम-ऑफ-कॉन्शियसनेस कविता

**पर्दे जो जानते हैं**

फीता उसकी पसंद थी, है ना, वो पैटर्न
छेदों का जो फूल होने का नाटक करते हैं, और मैं
तीसरी कतार में बैठी हूँ मेरी पसलियाँ
ओरिगामी बना रही हैं, सिमटती जा रही हैं छोटी, और छोटी,
एक कागज़ की सारस जिसे किसी ने नहीं माँगा—

वेदी पर गुलाब, किसी ने उन्हें उगाया है,
कोई मिट्टी में घुटनों के बल बैठा था खून बहाते हुए
सोचते हुए *ये किसी और की खुशी के लिए है*
जैसे मैं खिड़की पर तुलसी को पानी देती हूँ
जो फिर भी मर जाती है, हमेशा मरती है,

मेरे हाथों को उसके हाथ याद हैं
जैसे एक घर आग को याद रखता है
नवीनीकरण के बाद भी—
दीवारों में धुएँ की गंध,
कैसे तुम रगड़ते हो और रगड़ते हो और रगड़ते हो
पर लकड़ी की नस अभी भी काली है वहाँ जहाँ वो जली थी

उसका गाउन ऐसे हिलता है जैसे पर्दे हिलते हैं
जब कोई खिड़की खुली छोड़ देता है,
वो घरेलू साँस, वो अंदर-बाहर,
और मुझे याद आता है अपना बेडरूम,
धूल के कण अपना धीमा नृत्य करते हुए
दोपहर की रोशनी में, कैसे धूल बस
त्वचा है, बस वो है जो हम उतारते हैं और भूल जाते हैं,

क्या ये जलन है या ये शोक है
उधार के घूँघट में लिपटा हुआ—
मेरा पेट एक बगीचा है जो बीज बन गया,
खरपतवार जहाँ मैंने *ठीक हूँ* और *आगे बढ़ रही हूँ* बोया था,
मेरा गला एक दराज़ है जो अटक गया है बंद
हर उस बात के साथ जो मैंने नहीं कही

वो गुलदस्ता पकड़ती है और हँसती है
और मुझे याद आते हैं अपने हाथ, खाली,
हमेशा खाली, तनों की तरफ बढ़ते हुए
जो कभी मेरी दिशा में नहीं फेंके गए,

ऑर्गन ऐसे बजता है जैसे कुछ
पानी के अंदर हो, जैसे डूबना
संगीत में बदल गया हो, और मैं ताली बजाती हूँ
क्योंकि मुँह यही करते हैं
भले ही दिल
बस एक और कमरा हो
एक घर में जो धीरे-धीरे, चुपचाप,
बेचा जा रहा है

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental poem in the voice of someone who was not chosen, using unusual adjectives and unconventional grammar to convey grief and resignation.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Unchosen Register

not-picked, i wear my skin like
a waiting room. name called
somewhere else, some other
throat-shaped hallway.

they said *almost.* they said
*such a near thing, such a
nearly-thing you were.*

i collect my losing
in a jar labeled *maybe-glass,*
grief gone translucent-thick,
gone syrup-slow, gone
quietly furniture in the corner
of every room i enter now.

what does the body do
with an almost. where does
selected-not-me go
to grieve its own unselecting.

i practice the smile that means
*congratulations* while my hands
practice something else entirely—
some grammar of the fist,
unclenching, unclenching,
because rage is not
a color i'm allowed
to wear at this particular
funeral of my own potential.

was chosen. was not.
past tense already,
though the wound
insists on present,
insists on now-ing
its ache into every
future tuesday.

i am becoming fluent
in the language of *next time*
which is another way of saying
*not this time*
which is another way of saying
nothing, nothing,
the silence where my name
should have unfolded
like a flag, like a door,
like a yes.

so i fold instead. origami
of the overlooked. i make
myself smaller, more
foldable, more
easily set aside
on some shelf
of what-could-have-been,

dust already
practicing
its settling
on my shoulders,

already calling me
*old news*
already calling me
*done*

when I have not
even finished
being sad
about it yet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of literary flash fiction/poetry hybrid about unrequited love, incorporating odd similes (like hair in a drain) and a tone of bitter, poetic sincerity.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Drain Knows

I loved you like hair loves a drain—inevitable, clogging, unwanted but persistent, coiling in the dark pipes of your indifference until something backs up and someone has to notice.

You never noticed. Or you did, the way you notice a hangnail: briefly, with mild irritation, before returning to whatever mattered more.

Here is a fact: my heart is a parking lot at 3 AM. Empty, lit for no one, waiting for cars that took the highway instead. Here is another: you were the highway. You were always going somewhere else.

I want to tell you love felt like a held door—that grace of small anticipation, the held breath before someone walks through. But it was more like a screen door in summer, slamming each time the wind changed its mind. I kept standing in the frame, getting hit.

They say time heals. They have not met my particular clock, which runs backward, which insists on 2:14 AM the night you said *let's just be friends* like friends was a place you could set me down gently, like a bag of something breakable you didn't want to carry anymore.

I am not bitter. 

(I am the bitterness left in the bottom of the cup, the coffee grounds no one wants to swallow but everyone tastes anyway.)

I loved you the way a moth loves the porch light—not the light itself, maybe, but the idea of warmth, the desperate architecture of wings against glass, again, again, again, until the wings give out or the bulb does.

Mine gave out first.

You'll find this someday, perhaps, tucked in a drawer of things you meant to read. You'll recognize yourself the way you'd recognize a stranger's coat left at your party—*oh, that's not mine, I don't remember them staying that long.*

But you stayed. In me. Like hair in a drain.

Like water that has to go somewhere, and finds every wrong way first.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a modern confessional poem exploring themes of loss, longing, and self-deprecation, ending on an image of two separate heartbeats in different rooms.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Arithmetic of Absence

I have made a career of counting
what isn't there—the space
where your toothbrush stood
against the porcelain, the missing
weight on the left side of the bed,
still dented like an apology
that never finishes itself.

I tell people I'm fine
in the particular way that means
I've alphabetized my regrets,
I've learned the exact silence
that follows when I say your name
out loud to test if it still tastes
like something I deserve.

Self-pity is a language
I'm fluent in, the mother tongue
of men who confuse suffering
with depth, who mistake
their own reflection in a dark window
for someone finally looking back.
I know. I know.

I want to tell you I've changed
but I still leave the porch light on
past midnight, some old animal hope
that light means arrival,
that anything comes back
because you left it a way home.

I am not a good enough poet
to make this beautiful.
I am only accurate.

Somewhere across this city
you are sleeping or you are not,
your chest rising in a rhythm
I no longer get to witness,
and I am here, in this room
that still holds the shape of us
like a held breath,

two hearts
still doing the only thing
they know how to do—

beating, beating,
in rooms that no longer
touch.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
